title: Give Thanks
subtitle: Gratitude When Life Is Unfinished
tagline: Gratitude does not require a finished story.
headline: Gratitude When Life Is Unfinished
headline_sub: Thanking God Without Pretending Everything Is Good
seo_title: Gratitude When Life Is Unfinished: Thanks in Hard Seasons
seo_description: Give thanks in all circumstances does not mean calling every circumstance good. A Thanksgiving devotional for men carrying something unresolved this season.
og_image_alt: Gratitude When Life Is Unfinished: Gratitude does not require a finished story. TheWrkShop.

scriptures.text: Rejoice always, pray continually, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.
Do not be anxious about anything, but in every situation, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God.

Though the fig tree does not bud and there are no grapes on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though there are no sheep in the pen and no cattle in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will be joyful in God my Savior.

blocks.text: Notice the wording.
Give thanks in all circumstances.
Paul does not command believers to call every circumstance good.
There is a difference.
Scripture does not require pretending otherwise.
And remember who is writing. When Paul told the Philippians to bring their requests “with thanksgiving,” he was in chains.
Yet he practiced thanksgiving while his own life remained unresolved.
GRATITUDE IS NOT ALWAYS A RESPONSE TO CHANGED CIRCUMSTANCES. SOMETIMES IT IS TRUST IN THE MIDDLE OF UNCHANGED ONES.
That is a deeper kind of gratitude.
“I CAN’T BE THANKFUL UNTIL THIS SITUATION CHANGES.”
Consider a man praying for reconciliation.
The relationship remains strained.
Or a man praying for healing.
The diagnosis remains.
Or a man praying for provision.
The financial pressure continues.
Gratitude can feel out of place when suffering is still present.
But biblical thanksgiving is not a declaration that the suffering is good.
It is a recognition that God remains worthy of trust.
When circumstances don’t change, our attention often locks onto the outcome.
These are understandable questions.
But something can happen beneath them.
We start treating the outcome we want as the condition for trusting God.
WITHOUT REALIZING IT, WE CAN MAKE OUR GRATITUDE DEPEND ON GOD DOING WHAT WE EXPECT.
That is the battle before the battle.
Not whether we want relief.
But whether our confidence in God rests entirely on receiving it.
THANKSGIVING AND LAMENT CAN EXIST IN THE SAME PRAYER.
Habakkuk shows us how.
“Yet I will rejoice in the LORD.”
The Psalms do the same thing again and again: faithful people cry out in distress and keep turning toward God.
Philippians 4 invites us to bring our requests with thanksgiving.
We are not told to stop asking.
We are invited to ask while remembering who God is.
Gratitude does not erase sorrow.
It refuses to let sorrow become the only truth we recognize.

items: What unresolved situation has consumed my attention?
Have I postponed gratitude until I get a particular answer?
What can I truthfully thank God for today?
Can I bring both disappointment and thanksgiving into the same prayer?
Am I trusting God’s character, or only the outcome I hope He provides?

blocks.text: Name one unresolved burden.
Tell God honestly how it affects you.
Ask for what you want.
Then name one truth about His character you can thank Him for.
Don’t force an emotion.
Practice honest prayer.
Gratitude does not require a finished story.

Father, You know what remains unresolved. I bring You my disappointment, my uncertainty, and my desire for change. Help me thank You without pretending my pain is gone. Teach me to trust Your character while I wait for answers. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
Gratitude does not require a finished story.
Thanksgiving and lament can exist in the same prayer.
Unchanged circumstances do not mean God has become unworthy of trust.
Paul wrote “with thanksgiving” while in chains.
